rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a usable angle and a tempting overclaim: "Warby Parker pilots glasses in pharmacies, testing a new channel for eyewear distribution" stays inside the facts, while B's "testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a contest the update does not support. A also has sharper proof gates, especially "Hold Angle 5 (pharmacy) until the partner name is confirmed"; B has good bones, but it keeps reaching for drama it cannot prove.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" leans on company-history context not supplied in the update; the DTC contrast is useful, but this wording overstates the fact base.

"this is a scaled company choosing where to deploy earnings" overreaches. The update says Warby recently reached profitability, not that the 40-store push is funded by retained earnings or free cash flow.

"healthcare access reporter tracking where Americans can get optical care without visiting a specialty store" stretches the pharmacy pilot. The fact says glasses through a pharmacy chain, not exams or broader optical care in pharmacies.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker is testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a head-to-head performance test. The update only says a pharmacy partnership pilot exists.
"bets its future" is melodrama. Opening 40 stores is meaningful, but the update does not say the company's future depends on this expansion.
"retailers adding clinical services to drive foot traffic" assigns motive. The update says optometrist-staffed exams are expanding, not why Warby is doing it.
"won't say how much comes from eye exams" turns "not broken out" into a refusal. Don't write a prosecution headline unless someone asked and the company declined.
